source.title: To grok or not to grok: Disentangling generalization and memorization on corrupted algorithmic datasets
source.authors: Darshil Doshi; Aritra Das; Tian-Yu He; Andrey Gromov

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests coexistence of memorization and generalization on corrupted modular-arithmetic data, using a different setting and measures from the claim versions focused on natural datasets.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on modular arithmetic with corrupted training labels and uncorrupted held-out examples. It does not test the claim's natural-data setting. Cited results from other studies are not extracted as rows. IPR is a representation-periodicity measure, not magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.test_reason: The study tests memorization/generalization coexistence, batch-size effects at roughly equal epoch budgets, and dropout effects, mainly in a new setting of corrupted modular-arithmetic classification. Its width comparisons do not establish generalization beyond an interpolation threshold.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors find that corrupted-label memorization and clean generalization can coexist and can involve distinguishable neuron populations. In the main quadratic model, weight decay and dropout favor generalizing representations, while BatchNorm suppresses memorizing neurons through their weights. These effects vary across architectures, activations and losses. The stated algorithmic-data limitation should acknowledge the appendix's MNIST experiment.
record.recipe_differences: Uses modular arithmetic with symmetric label corruption and mostly quadratic-activation MLPs, rather than natural datasets and standard image or language benchmarks; studies train/test accuracy, phase diagrams, neuron IPR, and pruning.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with data fraction, corruption fraction, weight decay, dropout, batch size, architecture, activation function, loss, width, optimizer, and normalization. Very high weight decay can cause forgetting; small batches enhance inversion; effects differ across MLPs, Transformers, and MNIST.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing width from 500 to 5000 slightly worsens quadratic-network generalization but substantially improves two-layer ReLU-network phase diagrams.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Width effects on corrupted modular-addition learning depend on activation and capacity, without establishing behavior past an interpolation threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Three-layer ReLU MLPs fail to memorize the corrupted modular-addition training set even with dropout probability 0.05.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small dropout can impair training-set fitting in this architecture and task.

fits_no_version.finding: Small dropout permits Transformer coexistence, whereas probabilities above 0.1 do not help.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dropout's effects on corrupted modular-addition Transformers depend on its probability.

fits_no_version.finding: BatchNorm weights correlate with IPR despite similar neuron IPR distributions with and without BatchNorm.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: BatchNorm can suppress memorizing neurons through their output weights rather than eliminating their representations.

fits_no_version.finding: Pruning low-IPR versus high-IPR neurons selectively impairs corrupted-label fitting versus clean generalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memorization and generalization can depend on distinguishable neuron populations in corrupted modular-addition models.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to modular arithmetic with synthetic label corruption, plus one MNIST experiment; it does not establish the natural-data claim. Several phase-diagram comparisons are qualitative and provide no numeric test errors or uncertainty estimates. Width comparisons do not identify the interpolation threshold.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for additional phase-diagram cells, figure-only curves, or other settings whose outcomes are only summarized qualitatively; extracted representative outcomes and explicit text-described condition changes. Width comparisons are qualitative as stated in Appendix O.

untested.parts: Matched training on natural versus fully randomized labels, chance-level held-out performance under fully random labels, and the named CIFAR-10/ImageNet architectures and recipes.
A width sweep establishing zero training error and subsequent test-error improvement under convergence-controlled, unregularized training.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Held-out optimizer comparisons under limited versus broader tuning. Appendix E's optimizer-dependent forgetting argument does not provide this comparison.
Image and language workloads, a quantified critical batch size, and whether longer training or alternative recipes remove the penalty.
Convolutional classifiers, the very-small-training-set boundary, and removal of dropout together with weight decay under data augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled sharpness, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Influence-based selection and removal of memorized examples, random-removal controls, and retraining.

missing.what: The explicit activation-dependent dropout result: two-layer ReLU networks enter confusion even at moderate dropout probabilities. This material qualification is not captured by the three-layer training-fit row.
The explicit loss-dependent dropout result: CrossEntropy requires much higher dropout probabilities than MSE to achieve grokking or inversion. Record matched held-out comparisons where readable.

record.verdict_notes: No original-source exclusion applies. Partial or absent coexistence under added weight decay does not challenge V1's unregularized capacity claim. IPR is a periodicity measure, not sharpness; neuron pruning is not memorized-example removal. Phase classifications use 90% thresholds and should not universally be paraphrased as perfect accuracy.

versions.untested_parts: Natural datasets and the named CIFAR-10, ImageNet, Inception, AlexNet, and MLP settings; random-label held-out accuracy.
A width sweep locating the zero-training-error interpolation threshold and measuring test error across widths.
Image classification and language benchmarks; workload-dependent batch-size thresholds and comparisons holding epoch budgets fixed across the range of batch sizes.
The claim's specific fully connected and convolutional image-classifier regimes and small-training-set boundary.

rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network
rows.operation_detail: Trained on modular addition with corrupted labels and evaluated on uncorrupted held-out examples.
rows.measure: Training and test accuracy; coexistence phase means both are close to 100%.
rows.value: Both train and test accuracies are close to 100%.
rows.note: Shows memorization of corrupted training examples alongside generalization on clean held-out examples in this algorithmic task.
rows.check: Evidence for the coexistence component: near-perfect fitting of partially randomized training labels and near-perfect clean test accuracy in the same network. It does not reproduce the separate natural-label versus fully random-label comparison.

rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network
rows.operation_detail: Trained on modular addition with corrupted labels using weight decay and evaluated on uncorrupted held-out examples.
rows.measure: Training and test accuracy; partial inversion phase.
rows.value: Test accuracy near 100%; training accuracy below 100%, with some corrupted examples predicted using the true labels.
rows.note: Generalization coexists with incomplete memorization; test accuracy exceeds training accuracy.
rows.check: Only some corrupted labels are memorized. Weight decay 5 also places this result outside V1's unregularized recipe.

source_check.locator_found: Section 2, Partial Inversion; Figure 1(b); Appendix A.1; Figure 23(b).

rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network
rows.operation_detail: Trained on modular addition with corrupted labels using stronger weight decay and evaluated on uncorrupted held-out examples.
rows.measure: Training and test accuracy; full inversion phase.
rows.value: Test accuracy 100%; training accuracy plateaus close to 100(1 − ξ)%.
rows.note: The paper states that the network does not memorize corrupted examples in this phase.
rows.check: Generalization is present, but memorization of corrupted labels is absent; coexistence is therefore absent. This deliberately regularized condition does not challenge the unregularized coexistence result.

rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network
rows.operation_detail: Compared width 500 and width 5000 networks on corrupted modular addition under weight decay.
rows.value: Width N=5000 generalizes marginally poorly compared with N=500.
rows.note: The text describes the comparison qualitatively; it does not state the phase-diagram coordinates or numeric test errors.
rows.check: No interpolation threshold or convergence-controlled comparison is established. The evaluated wider subject is width 5000, with width 500 as baseline; the phase diagram includes zero weight decay as well as positive values.

rows.subject: 3-layer fully connected ReLU MLP
rows.operation_detail: Compared phase diagrams for two widths on corrupted modular addition under weight decay.
rows.value: Width N=5000 performance is described as drastically improved; confusion phase is largely eliminated.
rows.note: This comparison does not locate an interpolation threshold or report numeric test errors.
rows.check: Figure 30 compares the two-layer ReLU network with Figure 27, not a three-layer MLP. Improved performance includes elimination of a capacity-related confusion phase; neither width is established as beyond the interpolation threshold.

rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network
rows.stage_stated: trained for roughly equal epochs across batch settings
rows.operation_detail: Varied minibatch size without explicit regularization or normalization and compared generalization and inversion.

conditions.value: decreasing batch size; specific compared values not stated in this result description

rows.measure: Generalization and inversion in phase diagrams.
rows.value: Decreasing batch size enhances inversion, including without explicit regularization.
rows.note: Authors attribute the effect to implicit regularization from minibatch noise. This is not an image or language benchmark.
rows.check: Appendix F explicitly reports enhanced generalization as well as inversion. Appendix A supplies batch sizes 8, 64 and 256, roughly equal epochs, and square-root learning-rate scaling. The result should record these conditions rather than leave batch values unspecified.

rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network
rows.operation_detail: Added dropout while training on modular addition with corrupted labels.

conditions.value: varied; specific values shown in figure

rows.baseline: No dropout; phase diagram shown for comparison.
rows.value: Dropout enhances robustness to label corruption and facilitates better generalization in some settings; very high dropout produces a confusion phase.
rows.note: The paper describes a range of dropout levels and reports underperformance at very high dropout.
rows.check: The row combines beneficial dropout regimes and excessive-dropout failure, both anticipated by V6. Split these conditions. Figure 19 gives illustrative probabilities 0, 0.3, 0.6 and 0.9, although its training curves alone do not establish a test-accuracy improvement over zero dropout.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 3(b) and caption; Section 2, Confusion; Section 3.2; Appendix A; Figures 19 and 25.

rows.subject: 4-layer ReLU MLP on MNIST
rows.operation_detail: Applied dropout during training with label corruption.
rows.measure: Train and test accuracies in phase diagrams.
rows.value: Dropout is not as effective; increasing dropout hurts both test and train accuracies.
rows.note: The text does not give numeric accuracies or dropout values.
rows.check: Increasing dropout lowers test accuracy in this corrupted-label MNIST experiment. This qualifies where dropout helps; it does not refute the version's explicitly regime-dependent claim.

rows.subject: 3-layer ReLU MLP
rows.operation_detail: Applied dropout while training on modular addition with corrupted labels.
rows.value: Failed to memorize the dataset for any stated data fraction and noise level, even after an extensive hyperparameter search.
rows.note: The stated result concerns memorization capacity, not a numeric test-error reduction.
rows.check: Failure to memorize training labels does not establish dropout's effect on held-out error. The text reports failure even at probability 0.05, not a quantified test-performance comparison.

rows.subject: 1-layer Transformer
rows.stage_stated: trained for 3000 steps with 3 random seeds
rows.operation_detail: Applied dropout while training on modular addition with corrupted labels.
rows.measure: Coexistence phase and average embedding-layer IPR.
rows.baseline: Small dropout probability; exact value not stated.
rows.value: Dropout probability larger than 0.1 does not help; small dropout permits a coexistence phase.
rows.note: The statement describes qualitative phase behavior; the selected points are α=0.9 and ξ=0.1.
rows.check: The subject is a Transformer, outside V6's fully connected and convolutional classifier families. Coexistence and embedding IPR also do not by themselves quantify improvement in held-out error.

rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network
rows.operation_detail: Trained with BatchNorm on modular addition with corrupted labels.
rows.measure: Test generalization and memorization of corrupted training labels.
rows.baseline: Without BatchNorm; IPR distributions do not differ significantly.
rows.value: BatchNorm can bias toward generalizing representations; BatchNorm itself de-amplifies low-IPR memorizing neurons.
rows.note: The text says the IPR distributions do not exhibit significant differences, while BatchNorm weights correlate with IPR.
rows.check: The recorded value measures BatchNorm's association with neuron IPR and weighting, rather than reporting the train/test accuracy needed to establish V1's coexistence effect.

rows.subject: 3-layer ReLU MLP
rows.operation_detail: Trained with BatchNorm on modular addition with corrupted labels.
rows.value: BatchNorm has only coexistence phases and can perfectly memorize and generalize for small corruption fractions.
rows.note: The study reports this as a representative training curve and qualitative phase result.
rows.check: This directly reports coexistence, but with BatchNorm. It extends the coexistence component to a regularized recipe rather than reproducing V1's unregularized comparison.

rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network
rows.operation_detail: Progressively pruned neurons from lowest IPR upward in a coexistence-phase model.
rows.measure: Accuracy on corrupted training examples, uncorrupted training examples, and test data.
rows.baseline: Before pruning, near-100% accuracy on train and test data.
rows.value: Corrupted-example accuracy decreases; test and uncorrupted-training accuracy remain high; overall training accuracy plateaus around 100(1 − ξ)%.
rows.note: Removing low-IPR neurons selectively reduces memorization while retaining generalization.
rows.check: The experimental contrast is neuron pruning after training. It does not compare random-label fitting capacity with natural-label generalization, or remove memorized training examples and retrain as V8 requires.

rows.subject: 2-layer fully connected network
rows.operation_detail: Progressively pruned neurons from highest IPR downward in a coexistence-phase model.
rows.measure: Test accuracy and accuracy on corrupted training examples.
rows.baseline: Before pruning, near-100% accuracy on train and test data.
rows.value: Test accuracy declines while accuracy on corrupted training data remains high.
rows.note: Complementary pruning result; supports the paper's separation of generalizing and memorizing subnetworks.
rows.check: The experimental contrast concerns neuron pruning and functional separation of subnetworks, not a claim version's specified comparison.
